title_en: The Avengers: Doomsday Final Trailer Just Made Steve Rogers and Peggy Carter’s Happy Ending More Confusing Than Ever Ahead of the MCU Crossover
summary_en: We've been confused about Steve Rogers and Peggy Carter ever since Avengers: Endgame, and the final trailer for Avengers: Doomsday only raises further questions.
body_en:
In case you’re currently trapped in a deep, dark, GTA-shaped hole, the final trailer for Avengers: Doomsday has landed . This new trailer doesn’t necessarily reveal a lot about the plot of the film we didn’t already know, but it does give us a closer glimpse of two characters who are clearly going to be a big focus: Chris Evans’ Steve Rogers and Hayley Atwell’s Peggy Carter. In fact, it’s starting to look as though Steve is the main character of this massive ensemble movie.
That’s not necessarily a bad thing, especially for fans who have struggled to connect with the more recent superhero additions to the MCU. But it does highlight a problem the MCU has faced since Avengers: Endgame hit theaters back in 2019. Nothing about the strange new existence of Steve and Peggy makes much sense. Let’s try to break it down.
We have so many questions surrounding the fates of Steve and Peggy after the Infinity Saga wrapped, and many of them have been burning since the final moments of Endgame. In case you’ve forgotten, Endgame wraps with Steve gathering the Infinity Stones and embarking on a quest to return them to their rightful points in time and space. We never see that quest play out (not even the surely awkward reunion between Steve and Red Skull on Vormir). Instead, we quickly realize that Steve never had any intention of returning from that final mission.
At that point, a much older and happier Steve shows up to pass the Captain America mantle to Anthony Mackie’s Sam Wilson. This version of Steve has clearly been living out a quiet life in the MCU for decades, enjoying the civilian life he was robbed of after becoming Cap. In the film’s final scene, it’s revealed that Steve’s final stop on his Infinity Stone quest was to reunite with Peggy in the 1950s, allowing them to finally share that long-awaited dance.
It’s a heartwarming ending, to be sure, but also one that raises a lot of weird questions. Did Steve really run off and retire in the past? How did no one ever notice Captain America hanging around in a time when he’s believed to be a dead war hero?
The questions only get more pressing the further you dig into this ending. As far as we’re aware, Peggy married a man in the 1950s and had children with him. Did Steve just erase all that from existence with his choice? Where was he at Peggy’s funeral in 2016’s Captain America: Civil War? And what about all the metahuman and alien-related incidents that have unfolded over the years? Did Steve just sit out those battles when he could have been helping?
However much the former Cap deserves some peace and contentment, it’s hard to understand how his choice to go back and be with Peggy doesn’t completely throw the MCU’s timeline out of whack. But the same could be said for the Avengers’ actions in Endgame as a whole. We still don’t fully understand the rules and mechanics of time travel in the MCU. Based on the many conflicting answers the Russo Bros. and others have given over the years, we’re not convinced they do, either. And now that we’ve plunged headlong into the Multiverse Saga, things are only becoming more confusing.
It seems as though Marvel is making at least some effort to address these lingering questions and the general uncertainty surrounding Steve and Peggy with the climax of the Multiverse Saga. The recently released Avengers Endgame: Encore ends with an extended version of that final Steve/Peggy scene . This time, their tender dance is interrupted by the arrival of Tom Hiddleston’s Loki. Specifically, this is the alternate 2012 version of Loki who partnered up with the Time Variance Authority.
That’s a good start. Thanks to his adventures with the TVA, Loki has a pretty firm grasp on what is and isn’t permissible when it comes to time travel and multiversal shenanigans. We’re not clear on whether this version of Loki is from after the series finale of the show ( when he took his place on the throne of the multiverse ), or if he’s coming from some point during the middle of the series. But either way, he’s clearly there to put the kibosh on Steve’s plan to f*** up the timeline.
Or is he? It sure doesn’t look as though Loki forces Steve to return to his rightful time and place. Instead, the final trailer seems to suggest that the two lovers move house and set up a new life elsewhere. We’re guessing that elsewhere is Earth-828, aka The Fantastic Four: First Steps universe. Presumably, the idea is that Steve can live quietly in a world that has no Captain America to begin with.
Whatever the case, Steve and Peggy maintain their new life long enough to raise a preteen son. Only at that point do the FF finally take notice of a family who by all rights should not exist in their world.
Loki’s intervention eases some of the immediate questions raised by Steve’s actions in Endgame, but it raises new ones in their place. Why is Loki so willing to help Steve and Peggy cheat the rules when the TVA is notoriously pretty rigid about upholding the natural order of things? Why does booting these two to a different universe not violate the organization’s mandate, especially after everything we saw in 2024’s Deadpool & Wolverine and all that Anchor Being business ? At what point does the elderly Steve return to his home universe?
But what really has us confused is the implication that Peggy now disappeared from the MCU in the 1950s. She’s supposed to be a very important figure post-WWII. She was instrumental in the founding of S.H.I.E.L.D. and worked with heroes like Michael Douglas’ Hank Pym. Is all of that just erased now, along with Peggy’s previous marriage? How does that not have a cascading ripple effect across the MCU? And how does the scene in Endgame where Steve travels back and sees Peggy at Camp LeHigh work now?
All we can think is that Peggy left behind some copy of herself to take her place on Earth-616. Maybe a Life Model Decoy? Or maybe Loki used his illusion magic to create a Peggy doppelganger. That would still require either option to be real enough to have sex and give birth, mind you.
Again, we really don’t understand how time travel works in the MCU, and we’re not sure the people writing these films and shows do, either. The entire situation with Steve and Peggy is one giant mass of confusion and awkward questions.
The most we can hope for is that Doomsday builds on the fact that these questions exist and that Steve’s very post-Endgame existence is so unnatural. Perhaps Steve’s selfish choice is why the multiverse is beginning to collapse. It certainly seems to be the onus behind Robert Downey, Jr.’s Doom’s warning to the Avengers, “All of you have lived stolen lives, and now you must give them back.” He may be a jerk, but we suspect Doom has a legitimate grievance with the former Captain America here.
For more, brush up on every Marvel movie and series in development .
Jesse is a mild-mannered staff writer for IGN. Allow him to lend a machete to your intellectual thicket by following @jschedeen on BlueSky .
